# Notes Before the Steering Committee

*Written before the destination-brand tender goes out, and before anyone has commissioned aerial footage. Destination strategies assembled after the visual identity exists are not strategies. They are a justification for a photograph somebody has already licensed, and they have a way of committing us to volumes we then have to physically accommodate.*

---

## What the brief is leading with, and what it's actually about

The brief asks for a plan to attract more international visitors, with sustainability and community benefit as conditions on that growth. I'd gently invert it. Demand is the easy variable. It is also the one we control least and can least easily undo.

Marketing is the most reversible thing we will do this decade — a campaign can be switched off in a fortnight. Concrete cannot. A building permit signed in an afternoon is a fifty-year decision. A coastal road alignment is permanent. A dam is permanent. A village where the young people left in 2027 because the only jobs were four months long is not a thing a later campaign repairs.

Which suggests an uncomfortable ordering: the promotional work is necessary, visible, and the part our own institution is equipped to measure — so it will absorb most of the attention regardless of what I write here. The real effort belongs in the things that are hard to copy and impossible to reverse: **carrying-capacity numbers written down before the demand arrives; who holds legal title to the land; what we publicly refuse to build; the shape of the calendar; and where the tax actually lands.**

A beautiful coastline is not a competitive advantage. Every tourism ministry on the Mediterranean has turquoise water and a drone. What almost nobody has is a credible, verifiable *ceiling* — and I'd suggest that in five years the ceiling is the brand.

---

## An assumption I'd rather state than discover

"A region with significant natural beauty and historical sites" carries luggage. I'm going to write as though we mean **southern Albania** — the Vjosa valley, the Riviera between Vlorë and Sarandë, Butrint, Gjirokastër — because it's the case where the reasoning is most testable, and because being wrong in a specific direction is more useful than being carefully vague. If someone in the room knows we mean Georgia, or Oaxaca, or the Peloponnese, this is the cheap moment to say so. Most of the structure transfers. Perhaps a third of the specifics don't.

Why it's the interesting case:

- We are **late**, which is the single greatest asset in the file. The mistakes have already been made in public, next door, at a scale we can visit by car. Every argument we are about to have internally has an observable outcome eighty kilometres up the coast. That is a luxury Croatia and Montenegro did not have and we should not squander by pretending our situation is unprecedented.
- The **Vjosa** was designated a wild river national park in 2023 — one of the last free-flowing rivers of its size in Europe. The asset here is an *absence*: no dams. Absences are cheap to keep and impossible to recover.
- Two UNESCO cultural sites, an intangible listing (iso-polyphony) that is a living practice rather than a monument, and a hospitality norm — *besa* — which is currently free and can be commodified into nothing within a decade if we're careless.
- A land-tenure situation dating to the early 1990s: informal construction, contested and unregistered title, restitution claims. **This, not marketing, determines who receives the money.** If title is unclear when the demand curve arrives, it resolves in favour of whoever has lawyers.
- And a proximity problem worth naming: we are a short crossing from a mature, saturated destination. We can be its overflow car park — day-trippers, four hours ashore, a coffee and a fridge magnet, all the load and none of the yield — or we can be the thing people cross *to* and stay for. That choice is being made right now by default, in the absence of a decision.

---

## What the research will tell us, and what it can't

The deck will contain a number showing that a large majority of international travellers say they would pay more for sustainable travel. That figure is true, it is true everywhere, and it describes what people say. Stated sustainability preference is the most inflated variable in travel research, for the same reason stated health intent is: agreeing costs nothing.

The more useful question — which I'd put to the research team as a suggestion rather than a correction, since they'll arrive faster if it's theirs — isn't *what do travellers value*. It's **in what order are the decisions actually made**. For a large share of arrivals the flight is priced before the destination is chosen, which means aviation route policy is destination policy, and we are currently outsourcing our visitor mix to whoever negotiates the airline subsidies.

And a second question, which nobody will have asked, because it isn't a tourism question: **at what moment does a family in Qeparo or Vunoi decide whether to add two floors, sell to a developer, or leave?** That decision window is narrow, it's happening now, and it will determine the physical and social form of this region far more than our positioning statement will. Everything else in these notes is downstream of it.

---

## Ideas, grouped by the bet each one makes

I'd float these rather than propose any. Which ones people reach for unprompted will tell me more about the room than the ideas tell me about the region.

**1. The number before the demand — a bet on sequencing.**
Publish carrying capacities for the pressure points — Butrint, the Karaburun–Sazan area, specific beaches, the Vjosa's raft-launch sites, the historic quarter of Gjirokastër — *before* we spend a lek on promotion. Not as aspirations; as booked, ticketed, enforced daily limits with a named authority and a published methodology. The binding constraint is probably water and wastewater in August, not beauty, and the engineers already know the number. The unglamorous version of this idea is: commission the hydrology before the brand book.

The reason to do it first rather than second is not virtue. It's that the moment demand exists, every proposed limit becomes a fight against a constituency that has already borrowed money.

**2. Title, not training — a bet on who owns the asset.**
The most consequential tourism intervention available to us is probably a land-registration programme with free legal support in the coastal and river villages, plus a right of first refusal for resident cooperatives on state land leases. It photographs terribly. It has no ribbon-cutting. It decides everything.

A training academy for hospitality staff is the version of community benefit that institutions reach for, and it produces well-trained employees of someone else's hotel. Ownership produces heirs.

**3. The shoulder, not the summer — a bet on the calendar.**
August is already at or beyond capacity; growth there is negative-value growth. Every promotional lek should be spent on April–June and September–November — wild-spring river flows, the olive and citrus harvest, transhumance, walking weather, the empty amphitheatres. Route subsidies and any tax relief conditioned explicitly on off-peak load factors, not on total seats. The prize isn't more visitors; it's the same visitors distributed across nine months, which is the only thing that converts a seasonal job into a year-round one, and a year-round job is the only thing that keeps a twenty-six-year-old here.

**4. The river as product, not backdrop — a bet that legal protection is the scarce good.**
Sell the Vjosa on precisely the thing it is: undammed, unchannelled, the last of its kind at this scale in Europe. Which means the marketing asset *is* the legal regime, and the strategy has an unusual implication — our most important promotional act would be an irrevocable statutory bar on hydropower and gravel extraction in the catchment, published, with a monitoring body that includes people who are institutionally inclined to embarrass us.

Yes, this constrains an energy ministry. That fight is worth having in month one, in daylight, rather than in year six when a permit appears quietly on a Friday.

**5. The refusal — a bet that saying no *is* the positioning.**
Print the ceiling. Publish, at the same size as the logo, what we will not permit: no cruise berth expansion beyond a stated daily passenger figure; no beachfront all-inclusive enclaves; no more than a stated share of any beach under commercial concession; a building height and setback line on the Riviera with no discretionary exemptions. Nobody does this, because it forgoes announceable investment. In a Mediterranean recovering from visible over-construction, a government that visibly declines to sell everything reads as confidence — and confidence is the scarce signal.

It is also, boringly, defensible. Every sentence maps to a statute rather than to a mood.

I'd expect the most resistance to this one internally, which is one reason to put it in the room early.

**6. The village veto — a bet on consent as governance.**
Let the settlements set their own visitor caps, hours, and rules on filming, drones, entering courtyards, and photographing funerals — and tie a fixed share of the visitor levy to them by formula, not by application. Two consequences: the load becomes locally negotiated rather than centrally imposed, and heritage stays a practice rather than becoming a performance. On that last point — pay iso-polyphony singers as musicians on their own occasions, at fees they set, rather than commissioning a nightly forty-minute version for a hotel terrace. The staged version is what remains after the real thing has gone, and it earns less.

**7. The levy that visibly returns — a bet against the treasury.**
A per-night levy, hypothecated by law, with a published ledger at village level: this many nights, this much collected, this is the wastewater plant it paid for. The fiscal authorities will object to hypothecation on principle, and they'll be half right in general and wrong here, because the entire political viability of restraint depends on residents being able to *see* that the visitors are paying for the pipes. Untraceable revenue produces resentment, and resentment eventually produces a government elected to remove the caps.

---

## What I'd measure instead of arrivals

Arrivals is the one number that can rise while everything else deteriorates, which is presumably why it's the headline. I'd keep it in the appendix and lead with: local retention of visitor spend per night; off-peak share of bed-nights; bed-nights per resident at the settlement level; August water abstraction and wastewater compliance; share of frontline roles that are local, permanent and year-round; median return visit rate; and net change in registered local ownership of accommodation. Also, quietly, the number of building permits issued outside the published envelope — the only leading indicator that matters, and the one that will be hardest to obtain.

---

## Three things that would change my mind

If the water and wastewater engineering turns out to be a solvable capital problem rather than a hard ceiling, the capacity argument weakens considerably and I'd rewrite most of this.

If day-visitor yield from the neighbouring island is materially higher than I assume, the overflow-car-park scenario is worth pricing rather than dismissing.

And if the land-title situation is more resolved than I think, item two drops from first place, which would be the best news in the file.

---

*One procedural note. Everything above is reversible except the physical decisions, and the physical decisions are being made this year whether or not this committee addresses them. So I'd suggest the promotional tender slips a quarter and the hydrology, the title survey and the building envelope go first. Someone will say that's not what we were asked for. That's fair. It's what I'd want to be able to point to in ten years.*
